title: Book Store API, part 2
idea: `PUT` replaces a whole book and `DELETE` removes one. Each handler rejects a missing book or bad input first, then changes the data.
points: `PUT /books/:id` replaces the whole book, so send title, author and year again.
`DELETE` answers `204` with no body; a repeat `DELETE` finds nothing and answers `404`.
Take `id` from the URL on `PUT`; never trust an `id` in the body.
Test every route, including the failures, then check what the store now holds.

steps.caption: A `PUT` arrives. The handler first looks the book up with `bookIndex`.
No book has that id: `findIndex` gave -1. The handler replies `404` and returns.
The book exists, so the handler checks the body next.
Missing or wrong fields: reply `400` and return. The stored book stays as it was.
A valid body replaces the book and keeps its `id`; the reply is `200` with the new book.
`DELETE` shares this first check and the `404`. If the book exists, `splice` removes it and the reply is `204`.

walk.text: Part 1, unchanged: store, helpers, `express.json()` and the `GET` and `POST` routes.
`PUT`: look the book up first, then validate. Rebuild it from the URL `id` and named fields.
`DELETE`: a missing book is a 404 before `splice` runs. Success is 204 with no body.
`call` sends one JSON request and prints the method, path, status and body.
Create a book with a wrong year, then fix it with `PUT`. The body's `id: 99` is ignored.
Failure paths: bad body, missing book, then `DELETE` twice. Expect 400, 404, 204, 404.
Check the data too: the seed ids must survive. Then close the server.

code.title: The delete trap
code.caption: No book has id 9, yet one disappears. Add a guard so a missing id removes nothing.

pitfalls: `splice(-1, 1)` deletes the last item: check `findIndex` for `-1` first.
A `404` on `DELETE` must leave the list unchanged; check the data, not only the status.
Malformed JSON gets Express's HTML error page; error middleware, covered later, fixes that.

quiz.why: `'2' === 2` is false, so `findIndex` returns -1. `splice(-1, 1)` then removes the last book, leaving two.

takeaway: Reject first, change last, and test the failures as well as the successes.

starters: What happens if the client sends invalid JSON?
Why does `DELETE` return 204 instead of the deleted book?
How do I test my API without writing fetch code?
